title: Mandoline Slicer for Small Batch Pickling: Quick Dill Cucumber Slices
meta_description: Master small batch pickling with a mandoline for perfect, restaurant-thin cucumber slices. Get our quick dill pickle recipe and pro slicing tips.
html:
There is something incredibly satisfying about a jar of homemade pickles sitting in the fridge. However, most canning guides assume you have a backyard garden full of cucumbers and a dozen quart jars ready to go. For those of us who prefer a few fresh jars at a time, small batch pickling mandoline techniques make the process fast and fuss-free.

The secret to a professional-looking pickle isn't the brine—it's the cut. When slices are uneven, some pieces stay crunchy while others get mushy. To get that consistent, deli-style look, I rely on a Mandoline Slicer. It removes the tedious knife work and ensures every single slice is the exact same thickness, which is critical for an even brine soak.

Why Use a Mandoline Slicer for Small Batch Pickling?

When you're only pickling two or three cucumbers, it's easy to think a chef's knife is enough. But if you've ever tried to slice a rolling cucumber into paper-thin rounds, you know it's a struggle. A Mandoline Slicer allows for restaurant-thin, even slices of veggies and fruit fast, which means your cucumbers will absorb the vinegar and dill more efficiently.

Consistency matters because of surface area. Thin, uniform slices create more surface area for the brine to cling to, resulting in a more intense flavor profile in a shorter amount of time. Plus, these adjustable mandolines with hand guards keep your fingers safe, which is a huge win when you're working quickly in a home kitchen.

Quick Dill Cucumber Slices: The Recipe

This recipe is designed for a "refrigerator pickle," meaning no boiling water baths or complicated canning equipment. Just fresh ingredients and a few minutes of prep.

Ingredients:

  • 2 medium English cucumbers (these have thinner skins and fewer seeds)
  • 1 cup white distilled vinegar
  • 1 cup water
  • 1 tablespoon kosher salt
  • 1 tablespoon sugar
  • 3 cloves garlic, smashed
  • Fresh dill sprigs and black peppercorns

Instructions:

  1. Wash your cucumbers and pat them dry.
  2. Set your Mandoline Slicer to your preferred thickness (I recommend 1/8 inch for a classic chip style).
  3. Using the hand guard, slice the cucumbers evenly from end to end.
  4. Pack the slices tightly into two clean pint-sized mason jars, tucking in the garlic, dill, and peppercorns.
  5. Whisk the vinegar, water, salt, and sugar in a small pot over medium heat until the solids dissolve.
  6. Pour the hot brine over the cucumbers, leaving about half an inch of headspace.
  7. Seal the jars and refrigerate. They are ready to eat in 24 hours.

Pro Tips for Small Batch Pickling Mandoline Success

To get the most out of your equipment, start by choosing the right cucumber. English or Persian cucumbers are ideal because they don't require peeling. If you use a standard garden cucumber, you might want to peel strips of the skin off first to ensure the brine penetrates the vegetable fully.

Always use the hand guard provided with your Mandoline Slicer. It might feel clunky at first, but it is non-negotiable for safety. As you reach the end of the cucumber, the guard prevents your fingertips from getting too close to the blade.

If you want to experiment with different textures, adjust the blade. A thicker slice creates a heartier, crunchier pickle, while a paper-thin slice is perfect for topping burgers or sandwiches where you want the pickle to fold and drape.

Cleaning and Maintenance for Your Slicer

Acids from cucumbers and vinegar can be tough on kitchen tools if left to sit. After your small batch pickling session, rinse your mandoline immediately under warm water. Use a soft brush to clear any cucumber bits from the adjustable blade mechanism.

Avoid using abrasive steel wool on the plastic housing of the slicer, as this can create scratches where food particles can hide. A simple dish soap and sponge will keep your tool in restaurant-grade condition for years.

Beyond the Cucumber: Other Quick-Pickled Veggies

Once you've mastered the cucumber, you can use the same setup for other vegetables. Red onions are a fan favorite; slicing them paper-thin with a mandoline transforms them from pungent to sweet and tangy, making them the perfect taco topping.

Carrots and radishes also work beautifully. For carrots, use a slightly thicker setting on the Mandoline Slicer to keep some "snap" in the vegetable. The uniformity ensures that whether you're making a quick slaw or a jar of pickled carrots, every bite tastes exactly the same.

FAQ

How long do these refrigerator pickles last?

Because these are not processed in a pressure canner, they must be kept refrigerated. They generally stay fresh and crunchy for 3 to 4 weeks.

Can I use a mandoline for other types of pickling?

Absolutely. Whether you are doing small batch pickling for onions, jalapeños, or zucchini, a mandoline ensures the pieces are uniform, which is the key to professional results.

Why are my pickles soft instead of crunchy?

Softness usually comes from two things: using overripe vegetables or not using a consistent slice. Using a Mandoline Slicer ensures an even cure, and using fresh, firm English cucumbers helps maintain that signature crunch.
